references.text: The psalmist writes that God knows our thoughts from afar. Jesus demonstrates the same divine ability to know the thoughts of the heart, as shown by the expression 'εἰδὼς τὸν διαλογισμὸν τῆς καρδίας αὐτῶν'.
The Lord says that he searches the heart and tests the kidneys. Jesus' knowledge of his disciples' inner thoughts reflects this divine attribute ascribed to Yahweh in the Old Testament.
The Lord looks at the heart, not on outward appearance. Here Jesus shows the same ability to look into people's hearts and know their inner thoughts and motivations.
Matthew's parallel account where Jesus calls a little child to him and places it among his disciples as an example of humility and true greatness in God's kingdom.
Mark's parallel account where Jesus takes a child, places it among them, and embraces it to illustrate servanthood and who is the greatest.
The immediate context: the disciples were discussing which of them was the greatest, and it was this mindset in their hearts that Jesus saw through.
Continuation of Jesus' teaching where he explains that whoever receives this child in his name receives him, and whoever receives him receives the one who sent him.
Another example in the Gospel of Luke where Jesus knows people's thoughts – he knew what they were thinking when he healed the man with the withered hand on the Sabbath.

John testifies that Jesus knew all people and did not need anyone to testify about a human being, for he himself knew what was in humanity. This confirms Jesus' ability to know the thoughts of the heart.
Jesus refers to himself as the one who searches kidneys and hearts, which directly connects to his ability to know the disciples' thoughts in Luke 9:47.
